sections.title: Welcome to Meridian Works
sections.tags: mission, about, company, overview, headcount, offices, who we are, what we do
sections.body:
Meridian Works builds workflow software that helps mid-size logistics and manufacturing companies see exactly where their operations are stuck and fix it. Our customers are regional carriers, contract manufacturers and third-party logistics providers (3PLs) that move physical goods on tight margins.

Founded: 2016. Headquarters: Austin, Texas. Other offices: Chicago and London. About 15 people work fully remote.
Team size: about 240 people. Engineering 84, Sales 41, Customer Success and Support 46, Product and Design 22, Marketing 16, Finance and Legal 12, People and Workplace 11, IT and Security 8.
By location: Austin about 150, Chicago about 50, London about 25, remote about 15.

Mission: make physical operations as visible and fixable as software.
What that means day to day: every team, from sales to finance, exists to help a plant manager or dispatcher find a bottleneck sooner and fix it faster. When you're unsure how to prioritize, ask which choice gets a customer to that outcome sooner.

sections.title: Our story and timeline
sections.tags: history, founding, funding, series c, milestones, timeline, founders
sections.body:
Meridian Works began in 2016 when Elena Marsh and Ravi Menon, who had worked together at a regional trucking company, built a small dispatch tool to stop trucks from sitting idle at loading docks. Other carriers asked to buy it.

2016: Founded in Austin. First customer is a 40-truck carrier.
2018: Flow Map launches. We reach 10 customers and 25 employees.
2020: Bottleneck Radar launches, our first product that recommends fixes rather than only showing problems.
2021: Chicago office opens to be near manufacturing customers.
2022: Series B ($24M). Team passes 100 people.
2023: London office opens for our first European customers.
2024: Series C ($62M). We complete our first SOC 2 Type II audit.
2025: Dock Scheduler becomes generally available.
2026: Connect 2.0 ships. Team reaches about 240 people and about 310 customers.

Why it matters to you: many of the practices in this handbook, like writing decisions down and keeping meetings short, come from the years when we were 20 people and could not afford waste.

sections.title: Product overview: Meridian Flow
sections.tags: product, meridian flow, flow map, bottleneck radar, dock scheduler, connect, integrations, features, platform, what we sell
sections.body:
Meridian Flow is our platform. It connects to a customer's existing systems, builds a live picture of how goods and work move through a facility, and points out where things are getting stuck.

Flow Map: a live visual map of a facility or network showing shipments, trailers, orders and work in progress. It answers "where is everything right now and what is waiting?"
Bottleneck Radar: continuously scans Flow Map data, alerts customers to emerging delays and suggests likely causes and fixes, ranked by estimated impact.
Dock Scheduler: schedules inbound and outbound appointments at loading docks to cut trailer wait times.
Connect: the integration layer. Prebuilt connectors for common ERP, transportation management (TMS) and warehouse management (WMS) systems, plus an open API.

How customers buy: annual contracts priced per facility, with modules added as needed. Most new customers start with Flow Map and add Bottleneck Radar within their first year.
Who uses it: plant managers, dispatchers, warehouse supervisors and operations directors, not just IT.

Learning the product: everyone completes the Product 101 course in the learning portal during their first two weeks, regardless of role. You'll also get a demo sandbox account. Use it freely.

sections.title: Customers and market
sections.tags: customers, market, segments, competitors, industries, verticals, who buys, use cases
sections.body:
We have about 310 customers in three segments:
- Carriers and fleets: regional trucking companies that want fewer idle trucks and faster turnarounds.
- Contract manufacturers: plants juggling many customers' orders on shared equipment.
- 3PLs and distributors: warehouses balancing inbound and outbound freight against tight dock capacity.

Typical customer size: 1 to 30 facilities, 200 to 5,000 employees.
Typical first purchase: Flow Map for two or three sites, then expansion.

Why customers choose us: they can see value quickly (most customers find a measurable bottleneck within their first month) and the product is built for operations staff, not analysts.

How we talk about competitors: respectfully and factually. Never criticize a competitor by name in writing to a customer. If a customer asks for a comparison, use the approved comparison sheets in the Sales space in Notion, or ask in #sales-enablement.

Customer confidentiality: customer names may only be used publicly if the customer has approved it. If you are not sure, treat the name as confidential and ask Marketing.

sections.title: Our values in practice
sections.tags: values, culture, principles, behaviors, customers first, write it down, direct and kind, own the outcome, sustainable pace
sections.body:
Customers first. We win when a customer's operation runs better. In practice: read the ticket before you reply, ask what the customer is trying to accomplish, and follow up after a fix.

Write it down. Decisions and context live in documents, not in heads or DMs. In practice: if a decision affects more than one team, write a short doc. If you resolve something in a call, post the summary.

Direct and kind. Say the hard thing early and say it respectfully. In practice: give feedback within a few days rather than saving it up for a review; assume good intent, and ask before assuming.

Own the outcome. If you see a problem, you are allowed to fix it or to raise it. In practice: "that's not my area" is not a complete sentence. Find the right owner and hand it over properly.

Sustainable pace. We would rather go far than go fast for a month. In practice: no expectation to answer Slack at night or on weekends, and we plan quarters with slack in them. If you are regularly working more than about 45 hours a week, tell your manager. It means something is wrong with the plan, not with you.

Values are also used in hiring, feedback and promotion decisions, so you will see them come up in your reviews.

sections.title: Company strategy and 2026 priorities
sections.tags: strategy, priorities, okrs, goals, roadmap, growth, company goals, h2 2026, plan, vision, where are we going
sections.body:
Where we are: about 310 customers, about 240 employees, and a product suite that now covers visibility (Flow Map), diagnosis (Bottleneck Radar), scheduling (Dock Scheduler) and integration (Connect).

Our three priorities for the second half of 2026:
1. Win the mid-size 3PL segment. These customers have the clearest dock-congestion problem and the shortest sales cycle. Goal: 40 new 3PL customers by year end.
2. Make Connect 2.0 the easiest integration on the market. Goal: cut average customer integration time from 6 weeks to 3.
3. Grow what customers already pay us. Goal: net revenue retention of 112% or more, driven by Bottleneck Radar and Dock Scheduler adoption.

Company OKRs for Q4 2026 are in Notion under "Company OKRs" and are presented at the start-of-quarter all-hands. The Data tab has a summary table.

What we are not doing: we are not building a general analytics platform, we are not expanding to new industries this year, and we are not opening new offices. When you are choosing between two tasks, prefer the one that supports a priority above.

How your work connects: your manager can point to the team OKR that your work supports. If you cannot draw a line from your work to a company priority, raise it in your 1:1. Either the work is lower priority than you thought, or the plan needs fixing.

sections.title: How we make money and the metrics we track
sections.tags: revenue, pricing, arr, nrr, grr, metrics, kpi, business model, subscriptions, churn, margin, dashboard, financial metrics, how company makes money
sections.body:
Business model: customers sign annual subscription contracts priced per facility, with separate prices for each module (Flow Map, Bottleneck Radar, Dock Scheduler, Connect). Most contracts renew automatically and are invoiced annually in advance on net-30 terms. Implementation and training services are sold separately and make up a small share of revenue.

Metrics you will hear about:
- ARR (annual recurring revenue): the yearly value of active subscriptions. New ARR comes from new customers, expansion ARR from existing customers adding facilities or modules.
- NRR (net revenue retention): revenue today from customers who were customers a year ago, including upgrades and cancellations, divided by what they paid then. Above 100% means existing customers are growing on net. Our target is 112% or more.
- GRR (gross revenue retention): like NRR but ignoring upgrades. Shows how much revenue we lose to cancellations and downgrades. Our target is 92% or more.
- Logo churn: the percentage of customers that leave.
- Time to value: days from contract signature to the first measurable bottleneck found. Our target is 30 days.
- Support CSAT: customer satisfaction on support tickets, out of 5. Our target is 4.6.
- Sales cycle: days from first meeting to signature. Current average is about 75 days for mid-size 3PLs.

Where to see them: the Metrics Hub dashboard in Notion is updated every Monday morning. Company-level numbers are shared at the monthly all-hands. Some figures, such as detailed financials, are confidential. Do not share them outside the company.

Questions about a metric's definition: ask in #metrics-help or finance@meridianworks.example.

sections.title: Competitive landscape
sections.tags: competitors, competition, positioning, differentiators, win themes, battlecards, compare, alternatives, market, why us
sections.body:
We compete in four ways. No single vendor does everything we do, so most deals are against a category rather than one named company.

1. Analytics add-ons from large ERP, TMS and WMS vendors. Customers already own these and assume they are "good enough". Our answer: they show what happened, while we show where work is stuck now and what to do about it, and we work across a customer's systems instead of inside one.
2. General business intelligence (BI) tools. Customers often try to build their own dashboards. Our answer: dashboards need analysts to build and maintain them, and ours work out of the box for operations staff.
3. Point solutions, such as a yard management or appointment scheduling tool. Our answer: one connected view instead of several tools that don't share data.
4. Doing nothing or building in house. The most common competitor. Our answer: the cost of delay. Use customer results and the time-to-value numbers from the approved sales materials.

How we talk about competitors: factually and respectfully. Never criticize a competitor by name in writing. Never claim a capability we don't have. If a customer asks for a comparison, use the approved battlecards in the Sales space in Notion, or ask in #sales-enablement.
Competitive intel: if you hear something useful about a competitor (pricing, a launch), share it in #competitive-intel. Do not go looking for competitor confidential information, and do not use any you receive by mistake. Tell Legal instead.
Win and loss reviews: the Sales team reviews every closed deal over $50,000 in annual value. The findings are posted monthly in #win-loss.

sections.title: Customer stories and use cases
sections.tags: case study, customer story, success story, examples, lone star freight, brightline components, harborgate logistics, results, outcomes, references, use case
sections.body:
These three stories are used in training and sales. Names and figures are approved for internal use. Before using any customer name or number outside the company, check with Marketing.

Lone Star Freight (regional carrier, 140 trucks across Texas and Oklahoma). Problem: trucks waited an average of 2.4 hours at customer docks, and dispatchers found out late. Solution: Flow Map and Bottleneck Radar, connected to their TMS through Connect. Result: average dock wait fell by 31% in the first quarter, and they added Dock Scheduler six months later.

Brightline Components (contract manufacturer, 3 plants in Illinois and Ohio). Problem: orders for different customers competed for the same machines, and planners found out about delays only when a customer called. Solution: Flow Map across all plants and Bottleneck Radar alerts. Result: late orders dropped by 22% in the first six months, and planners spend about 5 hours less per week on manual status updates.

Harborgate Logistics (3PL, 9 warehouses). Problem: inbound and outbound trucks arrived at the same time, and docks jammed in the afternoons. Solution: Dock Scheduler with Connect integration to their WMS. Result: trailer turn time improved by 27% and overtime costs dropped.

What these stories have in common: customers found value within 30 to 45 days, started with one module, and expanded within a year. They are the pattern we describe to prospects.
Customer references: only Customer Success and Marketing arrange reference calls. Never offer a customer's name as a reference yourself.

sections.title: Diversity, equity and inclusion
sections.tags: dei, diversity, inclusion, equity, belonging, pay equity, accessibility, inclusive hiring, discrimination prevention, representation
sections.body:
Our commitment: we want people from many backgrounds to join, stay and grow here. We believe that teams with different experiences make better decisions for our customers.

What we do in practice:
- Fair hiring. Every role has a written scorecard. Interviews are structured, with the same questions for each candidate. Interviewers are trained before they join an interview panel, and every panel has at least two interviewers. Job posts state the salary range.
- Pay equity. Each year People and Finance review pay by level, role and location to find unexplained gaps and fix them. Results are shared with the leadership team and summarized for all employees.
- Promotion fairness. Promotion and performance decisions go through calibration so that the same standards apply across teams. Managers are trained to spot bias.
- Accessibility. Our offices are step-free, our meetings have captions available, and our internal tools must meet accessibility standards. You can ask for workplace adjustments at any time (see Accommodations and accessibility).
- Employee resource groups. Five ERGs are open to everyone (see Recognition, community and employee groups).
- Inclusive language. We avoid jargon that excludes people and write so that non-native English speakers can follow. Pronouns in Slack profiles are optional and encouraged, never required.

Measuring progress: we track representation, hiring and promotion rates, and retention across groups, and we share a yearly summary at an all-hands.
Speaking up: if you think a process is unfair or something excludes people, tell your manager, People or the anonymous Ethics Hotline (1-800-555-0142). We want to know.

sections.title: Community, sustainability and giving
sections.tags: sustainability, community, charity, giving, volunteering, environment, carbon, recycling, donations, social impact, green
sections.body:
Volunteering: every employee gets 2 paid volunteer days a year. Several teams organize group days each quarter, for example at a food bank in Austin and a park cleanup in Chicago. Log them in Rippling as "Volunteer".
Donation matching: the company matches your donations to registered charities up to $500 per year. Submit the receipt in Ramp under "Charity match". Political groups and religious organizations used for worship are not eligible.
Giving campaigns: each December the company runs a giving drive. The company donates an additional $25,000, split according to how employees vote.

Sustainability commitments:
- Offices: recycling and compost stations, reusable kitchenware, and no single-use plastic bottles. Our Austin and Chicago offices use renewable electricity.
- Travel: we ask you to choose video calls instead of flying where the outcome will be the same, and to book trains for routes under 4 hours where they exist. We offset business air travel emissions through a certified provider.
- Equipment: old laptops and monitors are wiped and donated or recycled through a certified provider. Never throw electronics in the bin.
- Customers: a large share of our customers' value comes from cutting idle trucks and wasted trips, which reduces fuel use and emissions. You can share that as part of the company story.

Ideas welcome: join #green-team to suggest or run an initiative. The Workplace team funds good ideas up to $1,000 each.

sections.title: Glossary and acronyms
sections.tags: acronyms, glossary, jargon, terms, definitions, abbreviations, what does mean
sections.body:
ARR: annual recurring revenue.
BDR: business development representative, a sales role that finds and qualifies new prospects.
AE: account executive, a sales role that runs deals to close.
CSM: customer success manager.
DACI: driver, approver, contributors, informed. Our framework for cross-team decisions.
DRI: directly responsible individual. One named owner for a task or decision.
EAP: employee assistance program (confidential counseling and support).
ERG: employee resource group.
HSA: health savings account.
NRR: net revenue retention, a measure of how much revenue we keep and grow from existing customers.
OKR: objectives and key results, how we set quarterly goals.
PEPM: per employee per month.
PIP: performance improvement plan.
PTO: paid time off.
QBR: quarterly business review, a meeting between a CSM and a customer.
RFC: request for comments, the format for proposing engineering changes.
SLA: service level agreement, our commitment to response times.
SOC 2: an independent security audit report that customers ask us for.
TMS / WMS / ERP: transportation management, warehouse management and enterprise resource planning systems, the customer systems Meridian Flow connects to.
Sev 1 to Sev 4: severity levels for production incidents.
1:1: a regular one-on-one meeting between you and your manager.

sections.title: Your first week
sections.tags: first week, day one, first day, orientation, onboarding schedule, day 1, welcome call, buddy, what to do, start
sections.body:
Day 1: Pick up your laptop and badge at the front desk (or receive them by courier if you are remote). Meet your manager and your onboarding buddy. Join the 10:00am Central new-hire welcome call. Set up email, Slack, Okta and your password manager with IT.
Day 2: Complete the required training modules in the learning portal: Security Basics, Code of Conduct and Data Privacy. They take about 90 minutes in total and are due by the end of your first week.
Day 3: Shadow teammates, read your team's Notion home page, and set up 1:1s with each person on your immediate team.
Day 4: Meet People (HR) for a benefits walkthrough. Complete payroll and tax forms if you haven't already.
Day 5: Friday check-in with your manager: what is confusing, what is going well, and what you need next week.

Your onboarding buddy is a peer, not your manager, who is assigned to answer the small questions. Ask them anything. Meet them on day 1 and check in weekly for your first month.

Before you start: you should receive an email from People about 5 business days before your start date with your schedule, what to bring (I-9 documents, see Employment basics) and a link to set up your Rippling account.

If your laptop or accounts are not ready on day 1, tell your manager and IT right away. Do not wait. It is our mistake, not yours, and it will be fixed within one business day.

sections.title: First 30, 60 and 90 days
sections.tags: 30 60 90, goals, ramp, probation, expectations, milestones, check-in, first three months
sections.body:
Days 1 to 30, Learn. Understand the product, customers and team. Ship or complete one small, real piece of work. Meet at least 8 people outside your immediate team (coffee chats count; you can expense a coffee up to $10). Complete Product 101 and all required training.
Days 31 to 60, Contribute. Own a defined piece of work with your manager's guidance. Share one thing you think could be improved and how.
Days 61 to 90, Own. Work independently on your core responsibilities. Agree goals for the next quarter with your manager.

Check-ins: at day 30, 60 and 90 you have a short conversation with your manager and a People partner. These are conversations about how it is going, not evaluations. They cover what you have learned, what is blocking you, and how you are settling in.

Written plan: in week 1 your manager will share a one-page 30/60/90 plan in Notion. You are expected to edit it with them, not just receive it.

First formal review: your first performance review is in the next regular cycle (June or December) after you have been here 90 days. New hires are not compared against people who have been here for years. Your review focuses on ramp progress.

There is no formal probationary period at Meridian Works. Employment is at will, but concerns about performance are raised early and in writing, well before any serious step.

sections.title: Onboarding buddy guide
sections.tags: buddy, onboarding buddy, new hire buddy, be a buddy, buddy program, welcome, peer support, help a new hire
sections.body:
Every new hire gets an onboarding buddy. You may be asked to be one after you have been here for at least 6 months. This section explains the role, so new hires also know what to expect.

What a buddy is: a peer, not a manager, who answers the small questions, makes introductions and explains how things really work. A buddy is not responsible for the new hire's performance or training plan.

What buddies do:
- Day 1: meet the new hire in person or on video, take them to lunch or a coffee, and show them around (the office or the Slack channels and Notion pages).
- Week 1: a 15-minute check-in every day or two. Point them to the required training and answer "where do I find..." questions.
- Weeks 2 to 4: a weekly 30-minute check-in. Introduce them to at least 3 people outside their team.
- Day 30: a short "how is it going?" conversation. If the new hire shares a problem, encourage them to tell their manager or People, and do not keep it to yourself unless it is minor.

Time commitment: about 2 hours a week in the first month. It counts as real work, so tell your manager. Buddies get a $50 lunch budget for the first week, expensed in Ramp.
Good buddy habits: explain acronyms, say "I don't know, let's find out", share your own early mistakes, and never gossip.
Confidentiality: if a new hire tells you about a serious concern (harassment, safety, a policy violation), do not promise to keep it secret. Encourage them to contact People, and tell People yourself if they ask you to.
Sign up: to volunteer, tell People (people@meridianworks.example).

sections.title: Interns and early-career program
sections.tags: intern, internship, summer program, early career, new grad, graduate, campus, conversion, apprentice, student
sections.body:
Meridian Works runs a 12-week summer internship in Austin and Chicago, and a smaller winter program. Interns are employees and follow this handbook.

What interns do: each intern joins a team, has a manager and an onboarding buddy, and works on a defined project with a clear outcome that is presented at the end. Past projects include a dashboard for support teams, a new onboarding tutorial and a data-quality tool.
Pay and benefits: interns are paid hourly (non-exempt) and record their time in Rippling. They receive the 2 paid company holidays that fall in the program, accrue sick leave, and can join team events. Interns are not eligible for PTO accrual, medical benefits or 401(k) matching, but can join the 401(k) and get the match if they work more than 500 hours. Housing is not provided. The program does include a one-time $500 stipend to help with start-up costs, paid with the first paycheck.
Program structure: week 1 orientation, weekly intern lunches with leaders, a mid-program check-in in week 6, a project demo in week 11, and a final review in week 12.
Conversion: strong interns may be offered full-time roles, usually in the final two weeks. Offers depend on performance, business needs and headcount. Offers are given in writing, with at least 2 weeks to decide.
Feedback: interns receive written feedback at week 6 and week 12. They are encouraged to ask for feedback often.
Managing an intern: set a project plan in week 1, meet for 1:1s weekly, and do not give interns unsupervised access to customer data.
Contact: the early-career program is run by People (people@meridianworks.example).

sections.title: Onboarding for Engineering
sections.tags: engineering, developer, engineer, dev environment, first pr, on-call shadow, code, repo, setup
sections.body:
Week 1: Get your development environment running using the setup guide in the engineering handbook in Notion (target: a working local build by end of day 2). Get GitHub, AWS (read-only), Datadog and PagerDuty access through Okta requests. Meet your squad's product manager and designer.
Week 1 to 2: Ship a first pull request. It is expected to be small: a docs fix, a test, or a low-risk bug. The goal is to learn the review and release process, not to impress anyone.
Weeks 2 to 4: Take a starter ticket labeled "good-first-issue" in your squad's backlog. Pair with a teammate at least twice.
Day 30: Give a five-minute demo of what you shipped at your squad's weekly demo.
Days 30 to 60: Shadow the on-call rotation as an observer, without paging duties. Read three recent incident postmortems.
Days 60 to 90: Join the on-call rotation if your role includes it (see Engineering practices and on-call).

Access levels: production access is granted after you complete Security Basics and your manager approves. It is not automatic. Ask in #it-help with your manager tagged.
Laptop: a MacBook Pro by default. You may request an external monitor and keyboard.

Where to ask technical questions: your squad channel first, then #eng-help. No question is too basic in your first month.

sections.title: Onboarding for Sales
sections.tags: sales, account executive, ae, bdr, sdr, salesforce, gong, quota ramp, sales onboarding, certification
sections.body:
Week 1: Set up Salesforce, Gong and the sales engagement tools. Complete Product 101. Shadow at least 5 recorded discovery calls in Gong.
Weeks 2 to 3: Sales bootcamp (a live, instructor-led program held every other Monday): messaging, discovery methodology, demo skills and our qualification framework.
By day 30: Pass the product certification (a scenario-based demo to a senior AE or your manager). You may not run customer demos alone until you pass.
Days 30 to 60: Take over a small set of accounts or leads. Your manager reviews your first 10 calls.
Days 60 to 90: Full pipeline responsibility.

Quota ramp for Account Executives: 25% of full quota in month 1 to 2, 50% in month 3, 75% in month 4, 100% from month 5. Ramp details are in your commission plan.
BDRs: your activity and meeting targets are ramped over your first two months. Your manager will share the schedule.

CRM rules: every opportunity needs a next step and a close date in Salesforce. Update opportunities within 24 hours of a customer conversation. Deals that are not updated for 14 days are flagged in the weekly forecast review.
Approved materials: use only content from the Sales space in Notion. Ask Marketing before sending anything else to a customer.

sections.title: Onboarding for Customer Success and Support
sections.tags: customer success, support, csm, support engineer, zendesk, tickets, sla, onboarding csm, customer support
sections.body:
Week 1: Get access to the support desk, Salesforce (read access) and the customer health dashboard. Complete Product 101 and the sandbox exercises. Sit in on live support and at least 3 customer onboarding calls.
Weeks 2 to 4: Support team: handle tickets in the P3 and P4 queues with a buddy reviewing your replies. Customer Success: co-run onboarding sessions with a senior CSM.
Days 30 to 60: Support team: join the P2 queue. CSMs: take over a starter portfolio of accounts with a senior CSM as backup.
Days 60 to 90: Support team: join the P1 escalation rota once trained. CSMs: run your first customer QBR with a colleague present.

Ticket priorities and response targets (SLAs):
- P1 (production down, no workaround): first response in 15 minutes, 24/7.
- P2 (major feature degraded): first response in 1 hour.
- P3 (minor issue or question): first response within 8 business hours.
- P4 (request or feedback): first response within 2 business days.

Escalation: if you cannot resolve something within its SLA, escalate to your team lead, then to the on-call engineer through PagerDuty for P1 and P2.
Tone: always thank the customer, own the problem in the first sentence, and give a next step with a time.

sections.title: Onboarding for Marketing and Product
sections.tags: marketing, product manager, designer, product, design, content, brand, roadmap, figma, hubspot
sections.body:
Marketing:
- Week 1: get access to the content calendar, brand guidelines, the design library in Figma and the marketing automation tools. Read the last two quarters of campaign reports.
- By day 30: shadow a launch from planning to publication. Complete brand and legal review training (all external content needs review, see Social media and media inquiries).
- By day 60: own a small campaign or content piece end to end.

Product and Design:
- Week 1: join your squad's rituals (planning, weekly demo, retro). Read the current roadmap doc and the last three product requirement documents.
- Weeks 2 to 4: join at least 5 customer calls (Sales or Customer Success will invite you). Product managers and designers are expected to speak to customers every month.
- By day 60: lead a small discovery or design task with a written recommendation.
- Design files: keep work in the shared Figma team project, not personal drafts. Name files by squad and feature.

How we make product decisions: a short written problem statement, evidence from customers or data, options and a recommendation. Decisions that affect more than one squad use DACI (see Decision-making and planning).

sections.title: Onboarding for Finance, People and Operations
sections.tags: finance, people, hr, operations, accounting, legal, workplace, it, back office, month-end, payroll team
sections.body:
Finance:
- Week 1: get access to the accounting system, Ramp and Rippling in view-only mode. Read the month-end close calendar and the approval matrix (see Corporate cards, procurement and approvals).
- By day 30: shadow one full month-end close. Learn the expense and reimbursement flow end to end.
- Segregation of duties: nobody approves their own expense, payment or vendor. This applies to everyone in Finance without exception.

People (HR):
- Week 1: get access to Rippling admin (read-only until trained), the applicant tracking system and case notes. Complete confidentiality training. Anything you learn about a colleague through this role is confidential.
- By day 30: sit in on onboarding sessions, benefits walkthroughs and at least two employee-relations meetings as an observer.

Operations, Workplace and IT:
- Week 1: get admin access training for your tools. Learn the ticket queues and the response targets (see Equipment and IT support).

sections.title: Equipment and IT support

sections.body:
Laptop: standard is a MacBook Pro. Windows laptops are available for roles that need them (approved by your manager). Laptops are refreshed every 3 years, or earlier if a device fails.
Getting help: post in #it-help or email it@meridianworks.example. IT responds within one business day, and within 2 hours for anything that blocks your work. For urgent issues, say "blocked" in your first line.

sections.title: Pay and payroll
sections.tags: payday, paycheck, salary, direct deposit, pay stub, w-4, first paycheck, payroll, wages, tax withholding, pay schedule, when am i paid
sections.body:
Pay schedule: every other Friday by direct deposit. If a payday falls on a bank holiday, you are paid the business day before.
Pay periods: each period runs Saturday to Friday. You are paid the Friday one week after a period ends.
Your first paycheck: it usually arrives on the first payday after your second week and may be partial. If anything looks wrong, message People right away.
Setting up: add your bank details and complete your tax forms (federal W-4 and your state form) in Rippling before your first payday. Pay stubs and year-end tax forms (W-2) are in Rippling.
Changing direct deposit: update it in Rippling at least 5 business days before a payday for the change to apply.
Wrong amount: if you were underpaid, People will correct it on the next payday, or by an off-cycle payment within 3 business days if the underpayment is more than $500. If you were overpaid, People will contact you to agree a repayment plan.
Raises and promotions: compensation is reviewed once a year in March, alongside the spring performance cycle. Promotions can happen in the March or September cycle.
Bonuses: sales roles have a commission plan in the offer letter (see Compensation, levels and equity). Other roles may be eligible for a company bonus that depends on company performance. People will tell you if you are eligible.
Pay questions: talk to your manager about your role and pay decisions, and to People about payroll mistakes.
Pay confidentiality: you are free to discuss your own pay with anyone. Managers must not share other people's pay.

sections.title: Timekeeping, overtime and employment classification
sections.tags: overtime, exempt, non-exempt, hourly, timesheet, hours, breaks, timekeeping, salaried, flsa, meal break, lunch
sections.body:
Exempt employees (most salaried roles) are not eligible for overtime and do not track hours. You are paid for the job, not the clock. Managers should not expect a regular schedule above about 45 hours a week.

Non-exempt employees (hourly and some salaried roles, such as support and facilities) are paid for every hour worked and are eligible for overtime.
- Record your time in Rippling every day. Submit your timesheet by Monday 5:00pm Central after each pay period.
- Overtime: hours over 40 in a week are paid at 1.5 times your regular rate. Overtime must be approved in advance by your manager.
- Breaks: a 30-minute unpaid meal break for shifts longer than 6 hours, and a paid 10-minute rest break for each 4 hours worked.
- Off-the-clock work is not allowed. Checking work email or Slack outside your hours counts as time worked. If you do it, record it.
- If you are asked to work unrecorded time, tell People. That is against company policy and the law.

Your classification (exempt or non-exempt) is on your offer letter. If you are not sure, ask People. If your role changes, your classification may change too, and People will confirm it in writing.

sections.title: Compensation, levels and equity
sections.tags: salary bands, levels, equity, stock options, vesting, commission, quota, accelerator, raise, comp review, promotion pay, options, 409a, cliff
sections.body:
Pay philosophy: we pay competitively for the role, level and location band, and we aim for internal fairness. Salary bands are set for each level using market data reviewed each year. Managers cannot pay outside the band without approval from People and Finance.

Levels: each function has a career ladder with numbered levels (for example E1 to E6 in Engineering). See Career growth and levels.

Annual compensation review: every March, alongside the spring review cycle. Changes take effect on April 1. Ratings and pay are discussed separately, and your manager will explain how your pay was decided.

Equity: most employees receive stock options.
- Vesting: 4 years, with a 1-year cliff. 25% vests at your first anniversary, then 1/48th vests monthly.
- Exercise window after leaving: 90 days from your last day. Details are in your grant agreement and equity portal.
- Refresh grants: considered for high performers and at promotion. Not guaranteed.
- Questions about taxes: talk to your own tax adviser. The company cannot give tax advice.

Sales commission (Account Executives): a plan document is issued with your offer letter.
- Annual new-business quota is set by level (for example $1.2M in new ARR for a mid-level AE).
- Commission rate is 10% of new ARR at quota.
- Accelerators: 1.5x rate above 100% of quota and 2x above 125%.
- Commission is earned when the customer signs and the first invoice is paid. It is paid on the first payday after the quarter closes and collections are reconciled.
- Clawback: if a customer cancels within 90 days of signing for reasons within our control, related commission may be reversed.
- BDR pay is a base plus a bonus per qualified meeting that becomes an opportunity, described in your plan.

Any pay or commission dispute goes first to your manager, then to People.

sections.title: Pay bands and pay equity
sections.tags: pay bands, salary range, pay transparency, location tiers, market data, band, compensation philosophy, pay range, tiers, geo pay, pay fairness
sections.body:
How bands work: each level in each function has a salary band with a minimum, a midpoint and a maximum. You are placed in the band based on your skills, experience and the role. New hires usually start between the minimum and midpoint. Moving toward the top of the band takes sustained performance and growth.
Location tiers: bands are adjusted for where you live or are based.
- Tier 1 (New York City, San Francisco Bay Area): band +10%.
- Tier 2 (Austin, Chicago, Seattle, Boston, Denver): standard band.
- Tier 3 (all other US locations): band -8%.
- London uses its own UK bands.
If you move to a location in a different tier, your pay is adjusted on the first payday after your move, or at the next review. Moving to a lower tier is phased in over 12 months.
Transparency: you can see the band for your own level in Rippling under "Compensation". Managers can see the bands for their team. Job postings state the range for the role.
Keeping up with the market: bands are reviewed each January using survey data. Changes to bands are separate from individual raises. A band increase does not by itself change your pay.
Pay equity: each year People and Finance run a pay equity review by level and role. If unexplained gaps appear, they are fixed in the next review cycle. You can ask People to review your own pay.
Raises and promotions: see Compensation, levels and equity and Career growth and levels.
Discussing pay: you can discuss your pay with anyone. Managers must not share other people's pay.
The Data tab contains an example band table for Engineering and Sales.

sections.title: Benefits: medical, dental and vision
sections.tags: health insurance, medical, dental, vision, ppo, hdhp, premium, dependents, coverage, enroll, benefits start, insurance, deductible, coverage start date
sections.body:
Eligibility: full-time employees (30 or more hours per week) and their spouses or domestic partners and dependent children up to age 26.
Coverage starts: the first day of the month after your start date. Example: if you start on October 12, coverage starts on November 1.
Enrollment window: you have 30 days from your start date to enroll in Rippling. If you miss it, you can only enroll during open enrollment in November (coverage begins January 1) or after a qualifying life event.

Medical plans: choose between a PPO and a high-deductible health plan (HDHP).
- Meridian Works pays 80% of the premium for you and 70% for your dependents.
- The PPO has a higher premium and lower deductible. The HDHP has a lower premium and a higher deductible, and is paired with a health savings account.
- Both plans cover preventive care at no cost.
Dental: two plan tiers, with 100% coverage for cleanings and preventive care. The company pays 80% of the premium for you.
Vision: one plan covering an annual eye exam and an allowance for glasses or contacts. The company pays 80% of the premium for you.

Waiving coverage: if you have coverage elsewhere you may waive. You can enroll later only in a qualifying event.
Between start date and coverage: if you need care before your coverage begins, talk to People. Do not delay urgent care.
Questions about specific claims or providers: contact the insurance carrier using the number on your card. People can help with enrollment problems but cannot see your claims.

sections.title: Benefits: 401(k), HSA and financial
sections.tags: 401k, retirement, match, hsa, fsa, life insurance, disability insurance, financial wellness, employer contribution, vesting match, savings
sections.body:
401(k): the company matches 100% of your contributions up to 4% of your pay. The match is fully vested immediately, so it is yours even if you leave the next day.
- Enrollment: available after your first paycheck. Enroll in Rippling.
- Default: you are not automatically enrolled. You must choose a contribution rate.
- Traditional and Roth options are both available. You can change your rate at any time.
- Match timing: the match is deposited each payday along with your contribution.
Example: if you earn $100,000 and contribute at least 4%, you contribute $4,000 and the company adds $4,000.

Health savings account (HSA): available with the HDHP. The company contributes $750 per year, deposited in the first payday of the year (prorated in your first year). You can add your own tax-advantaged contributions up to the annual IRS limit. HSA funds roll over and are yours to keep.
Flexible spending accounts (FSA): available if you choose the PPO. Healthcare FSA and dependent-care FSA. Funds are use-it-or-lose-it up to the plan's limited carryover.

Life and disability insurance: at no cost to you.
- Basic life insurance: 1x your annual salary.
- Short-term disability (STD): 60% of pay for up to 12 weeks (see Medical leave, FMLA and disability).
- Long-term disability (LTD): 60% of pay after STD ends.
Optional: supplemental life, accident and critical illness insurance, at your own cost.

sections.title: Benefits: wellbeing, learning and perks
sections.tags: wellness, eap, counseling, gym, learning budget, stipend, therapy, mental health benefits, perks, volunteer, donation match, commuter, conference, training budget, courses
sections.body:
Employee assistance program (EAP): 6 free, confidential counseling sessions per issue per year for you and your household, plus legal and financial consultations. It is run by an outside provider and Meridian Works does not see who uses it. Call the number on the benefits page in Rippling or use the app.

Wellness stipend: $75 per month toward a gym, fitness app or wellness service, reimbursed through Ramp. Keep the receipt.

Learning budget: $1,000 per year for courses, books, conferences and certifications, with manager approval. It resets every January 1 and does not roll over.
- If you attend a conference, register through Ramp and share what you learned in a short Notion post or at a lunch-and-learn.
- Certifications you obtain are yours. If you leave within 6 months of a course costing more than $500, you may be asked to repay it.

Volunteering: 2 paid volunteer days per year. Tell your manager and log them in Rippling as "Volunteer".
Charitable giving: the company matches personal donations to registered charities up to $500 per year. Submit the receipt in Ramp.

Commuter benefits: pre-tax transit and bike-commuting accounts are available in Rippling for Austin, Chicago and London.
Home-office and phone: see Hybrid and remote work and Equipment and IT support.

Perks for everyone: snacks and drinks at the offices, Wednesday team lunches, a company holiday party each December, and an annual company retreat.

sections.title: Open enrollment and life events
sections.tags: open enrollment, qualifying life event, change benefits, marriage, baby, divorce, november, dependent, add dependent, change coverage, loss of coverage
sections.body:
Open enrollment: once a year in November. For 2026, open enrollment runs from Monday, November 2 to Friday, November 13. Changes take effect January 1, 2027. If you do nothing, your current medical, dental and vision choices roll over, but FSA and HSA contributions do not roll over. You must re-elect them.

Qualifying life events: outside open enrollment you may change your medical, dental and vision coverage within 30 days of a qualifying event.
Examples: marriage or divorce; birth or adoption of a child; a spouse or dependent gaining or losing coverage; a change in your employment status or your spouse's; a move that changes which plans you can use.
How: report the event in Rippling and upload supporting documents (for example a marriage certificate or a birth certificate) within 30 days. Coverage changes usually take effect on the date of the event.
Adding a newborn: report within 30 days. Coverage is retroactive to the birth date.

If you miss the 30-day window, you cannot add the dependent until the next open enrollment. People cannot make exceptions, because the insurance carrier sets these rules.

Contact People (people@meridianworks.example) if you are not sure whether something counts as a qualifying event. Ask before the 30 days pass.

sections.title: Expenses and reimbursements
sections.tags: expense, reimbursement, ramp, receipts, submit expense, approval limit, meals, per diem, mileage, personal expense, pre-approval, spending, how to expense
sections.body:
Ramp is our expense and card system. Most managers and frequent travelers get a Ramp card. Ask your manager if you need one.

Approval limits (per purchase):
- Under $100: no pre-approval if clearly work-related.
- $100 to $1,000: your manager's approval first.
- Over $1,000: manager and Finance approval first.
- Software subscriptions of any amount: need an approved software request (see Equipment and IT support).

Submitting: upload the receipt and pick a category in Ramp within 30 days. Expenses submitted after 60 days may not be reimbursed. Missing a receipt: submit the "Missing receipt" form in Ramp. It is allowed up to 3 times per year.
Reimbursement timing: out-of-pocket expenses are reimbursed within 10 business days of approval, by direct deposit.
Personal expenses: never put personal expenses on a company card. If it happens by accident, tell Finance and repay within 14 days.

What you can expense: work supplies, approved software, coffee chats during onboarding (up to $10), team meals with manager approval, wellness stipend ($75 per month), home-office stipend, learning budget purchases, and travel (see Travel policy).
What you cannot expense: alcohol (except at approved client or team events), personal entertainment, fines and traffic tickets, personal grooming, and gifts to colleagues above $50.
Mileage: business travel in a personal car is reimbursed at the current IRS standard rate.
Client entertainment: needs your manager's approval first and must list the client's name in the expense note.

Never split a purchase into smaller parts to stay under a limit. That is treated as a policy violation.

sections.title: Travel policy
sections.tags: travel, flights, hotel, navan, per diem, rental car, rideshare, business trip, lodging, airfare, booking, trip, conference travel
sections.body:
Booking: book flights and hotels through Navan so we get the corporate rate and can locate you in an emergency. Book as early as you can. Fares booked more than 14 days ahead are cheaper.
Approval: get your manager's approval before booking. Trips over $2,500 also need Finance approval.
Flights: economy class for flights under 6 hours. Premium economy is allowed for flights over 6 hours. Business class needs VP approval.
Hotels: up to $250 per night in most cities and $325 in New York, San Francisco and London. Choose a hotel close to your work location.
Meals on travel: a $65 per day meal allowance. No receipts needed. Do not claim meals that were provided (for example by a conference).
Ground transport: use public transit or rideshare. A rental car needs approval and the company's insurance covers rentals booked through Navan.
Baggage: reasonable checked baggage fees are covered.
Loyalty points: you keep your own points and miles.
Personal time: you may extend a trip for personal reasons at your own cost. Keep the personal portion on a separate booking.
Cancellations and problems: use Navan support (24/7) and tell your manager. If your trip is disrupted, keep receipts for extra costs and submit them in Ramp.
Travel safety: share your itinerary with your manager. In an emergency, contact Navan, then the security team at security@meridianworks.example.
International travel: needs manager approval at least 3 weeks ahead so IT can prepare your device and any required visas can be arranged.
facts: hotel per night ($325 NYC, SF, London)

sections.title: Corporate cards, procurement and approvals
sections.tags: approval matrix, purchasing, procurement, vendor, corporate card, ramp card, spend, contracts, purchase order, w-9, vendor onboarding, budget, signing authority
sections.body:
Company cards: managers and frequent purchasers get Ramp cards. Each card has a monthly limit set by Finance. Cards are for business use only.
Lost or stolen card: freeze it immediately in the Ramp app, then tell Finance (finance@meridianworks.example).

Spend approval matrix (per purchase or contract, total annual value):
- Up to $1,000: your manager.
- $1,000 to $10,000: your Director plus Finance.
- $10,000 to $50,000: your VP plus the CFO.
- Over $50,000: the CEO and the CFO.
Multi-year commitments are counted at their full total value.

New vendors: before purchase, a vendor needs a Security review (if it will touch company or customer data), a Legal review of the contract, a W-9 (US) or tax form, and Finance approval. Start these at least 10 business days before you need the tool.

Signing authority: only company officers (the CEO, CFO and General Counsel, or those they formally delegate in writing) can sign contracts for the company. You cannot sign a contract, order form or NDA on behalf of Meridian Works, even if a customer or vendor asks you to. Send it to Legal through #legal-requests. Legal responds within 3 business days.

Never accept a discount or gift from a vendor in exchange for a purchase decision. See Ethics and conflicts of interest.

sections.title: UK and London employee supplement
sections.tags: uk, london, united kingdom, bank holidays, pension, notice period, statutory, gbp, british, england, london office, employment contract, right to work
sections.body:
This supplement covers differences for employees of Meridian Works UK Ltd, who are based in London. Your employment contract is the final authority. If this section differs from your contract, the contract applies.

Holidays: 25 days of annual leave (pro rata in your first year), plus the 8 bank holidays in England, plus 3 company days (2026: Thursday, December 24, Tuesday, December 29 and Wednesday, December 30). That matches the 11 company holidays of the US offices. The leave year is January to December. Up to 5 days carry over.
2026 UK bank holidays: January 1, April 3 (Good Friday), April 6 (Easter Monday), May 4, May 25, August 31, December 25 and December 28 (Boxing Day observed).
Sick pay: company sick pay at full pay for up to 10 days a year, after that statutory sick pay rules apply. Self-certify for up to 7 calendar days.
Pension: the company pays 5% of your salary into a workplace pension if you contribute at least 5%. You are auto-enrolled after one month.
Private medical insurance: company-paid cover for you, with options for family members at your cost. Dental and optical are included at a basic level.
Parental leave: 26 weeks of full pay for the primary caregiver and 4 weeks of full pay for the secondary caregiver, plus statutory leave and shared parental leave rights.
Notice periods: one month during the first 6 months, and then 3 months for senior and managerial roles, or one month for others. Your contract states yours.
Pay: monthly, on the last working day of the month, in GBP. Expenses are claimed in GBP through Ramp. Mileage and per diems follow HMRC rules.
Working time: the standard week is 37.5 hours. Overtime for non-exempt roles is handled as time off in lieu, agreed with your manager.
Right to work: you must show original right-to-work documents before your start date.
Questions: contact People (people@meridianworks.example) or the UK People lead.

sections.title: Where we can employ you: states and registrations
sections.tags: states, remote states, registered, employer registration, tax, where can i live, payroll states, texas, illinois, new york, california, colorado, washington, work from another state, move states
sections.body:
We can only employ people in places where Meridian Works is registered as an employer for tax, payroll and insurance. This is why long stays in another state need approval.

States where we are registered (US): Texas, Illinois, New York, California, Colorado, Washington, Massachusetts, Georgia, North Carolina, Florida and Ohio. We also employ people in England through our UK company.
If you live in one of these places, you can work from home there. If you want to move to a place that is not on this list, talk to People before you move. We may not be able to employ you in a new place, or registration can take 4 to 8 weeks.

Short stays in another state: up to 2 weeks in a calendar year needs only your manager's knowledge. Longer stays need manager and People approval, because they can create tax obligations for you and for us.
Moving within our registered states: tell People at least 30 days before you move so they can update payroll, tax withholding and benefits. You may need to change your health plan options, as plans vary by state.
What changes when you move: state income tax withholding, state leave laws (where they give you more than the company policy, you get the more generous), final-pay rules, and your location pay band (see the Data tab for pay bands).
Where local law gives you more: our policies are designed to meet or exceed legal requirements. If state or local law gives you a better right than this handbook, you get the better right. Examples include paid sick leave and pay transparency.
Questions: people@meridianworks.example.

sections.title: Time off: PTO and sick leave
sections.tags: pto, vacation, time off, days off, sick days, sick leave, carryover, accrue, request time off, holiday, floating holiday, how many days, paid time off
sections.body:
Paid time off (PTO): full-time employees get 20 days per year, accrued every pay period (about 0.77 days). New employees can use accrued PTO from day one. Part-time employees accrue on a prorated basis.
Carryover: unused PTO carries over up to 5 days into the next year. Anything above 5 days is lost on December 31.
Requesting: request time off in Rippling. For anything longer than 3 days, request at least 2 weeks in advance. Your manager approves it, usually within 2 business days. Check with your team so critical work is covered.
Payout: unused PTO is paid out when you leave only where required by state law (for example California). See Leaving the company.
No-blackout policy: there are no blackout dates, but some teams have busy periods (for example quarter-end for Sales and Finance) where managers may ask you to plan around them.

Sick leave: 10 paid sick days per year, separate from PTO. Use them for your own illness or injury, medical appointments, or to care for a family member. Tell your manager the morning you are out. You do not need a doctor's note for absences shorter than 4 days. For 4 or more consecutive days, People may ask for confirmation from a health provider. Sick leave does not carry over.
Floating holidays: 2 per year, for any day that matters to you (see Company holidays 2026). Request them in Rippling as "Floating holiday".
Time off in your first weeks: you may take planned time off in your first 90 days. Tell your manager before you accept the offer if you have booked travel.
Unplanned absences: if you cannot reach your manager, message your team channel and People.

sections.title: Parental leave
sections.tags: parental leave, maternity, paternity, baby, adoption, foster, primary caregiver, secondary caregiver, newborn, new parent, childbirth, bonding, return to work
sections.body:
Meridian Works offers paid parental leave for births, adoptions and foster placements.
- Primary caregiver: 16 weeks of paid leave at 100% of your pay.
- Secondary caregiver: 8 weeks of paid leave at 100% of your pay.
You decide which applies to you. Both parents can take leave if both work here.

Eligibility: all full-time employees, from your first day. There is no waiting period.
When: leave can start any time within the first 12 months after the birth, adoption or placement. It can be taken in one block or in up to 2 blocks (the second block must start within 12 months).
Birth parents: any medical recovery time is part of the leave, not in addition to it. Short-term disability may run at the same time (see Medical leave, FMLA and disability).
Notice: tell People at least 30 days beforehand when possible, or as soon as you can. Then People will send you the leave paperwork and coordinate with your manager on coverage.
Benefits during leave: your health coverage continues on the same terms, and vesting of equity continues.
Raises and reviews: your annual review and raise are not reduced because you were on leave.
Returning: you return to the same or an equivalent role. Ramp-back is flexible. Many people work four-day weeks for the first 2 weeks. Talk to your manager and People.
Lactation support: private rooms are available in each office. Ask Workplace. Remote employees can get help with pumping supplies through the wellness stipend.
Fertility, adoption and surrogacy: talk to People about benefits and support available through your medical plan.

sections.title: Medical leave, FMLA and disability
sections.tags: fmla, medical leave, disability, short-term disability, std, ltd, illness, surgery, family leave, caregiver leave, accommodation, workers comp, injury, long-term, health leave
sections.body:
FMLA (Family and Medical Leave Act): if you have worked here at least 12 months and at least 1,250 hours in the last 12 months, you may be eligible for up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in a 12-month period for your own serious health condition, to care for a spouse, child or parent with a serious health condition, or for bonding with a new child. Your benefits continue during FMLA leave.
Company medical leave: if you do not yet qualify for FMLA, People will work with you on a leave, and state laws may apply.

Short-term disability (STD): pays 60% of your pay for up to 12 weeks for a non-work illness, injury, pregnancy or recovery, after a 7-day waiting period. You can use sick days or PTO during the waiting period. Apply through the insurance carrier. People will help you start the claim.
Long-term disability (LTD): pays 60% of pay after STD ends, up to a monthly maximum. Details are in the benefits summary in Rippling.

How to request leave: contact People (people@meridianworks.example) as early as possible. You do not need to explain your medical details to your manager. You only share what you choose. People will handle documentation and tell your manager only that you will be out, and the dates.
Reasonable accommodations: if you have a disability or a medical condition that affects how you work, you can request an accommodation through People. Requests are confidential and are handled in good faith, and People will work with you on options. You cannot be treated worse for asking.
Workplace injuries: report any injury at work to your manager and People within 24 hours, even if it seems minor. Workers' compensation covers work-related injuries and illnesses.
Privacy: medical information is kept separate from your personnel file and shared only with people who need it to support you.

sections.title: Other leave: bereavement, jury duty, military, sabbatical and personal
sections.tags: bereavement, funeral, jury duty, voting, military leave, sabbatical, personal leave, unpaid leave, family death, witness, reserve, five years
sections.body:
Bereavement: 5 paid days for the death of an immediate family member (spouse or partner, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, or in-law) and 2 paid days for extended family or a close friend. Tell your manager and record it in Rippling as "Bereavement". If you need more time, talk to your manager and People. Use PTO or ask about unpaid leave.
Jury duty and court: paid time off for jury duty or when you are subpoenaed as a witness. Give your manager a copy of the summons as soon as you get it.
Voting: up to 2 paid hours off to vote if your work hours make it hard to vote outside of work.
Military leave: paid and unpaid leave is available for reserve and National Guard service, following the federal USERRA law. Tell People as soon as you get orders.
Sabbatical: after 5 years of service, employees get a paid 4-week sabbatical, which can be combined with 2 weeks of PTO. Plan it with your manager at least 3 months ahead.
Personal leave: after 12 months, you may request up to 4 weeks of unpaid personal leave, subject to manager and People approval. Benefits continue if you pay your share of the premium.
Religious observance: use floating holidays or PTO. If you need a schedule adjustment, talk to your manager or People.
Time off to donate blood or take part in disaster relief: talk to your manager. Reasonable time is fine.

sections.title: Hybrid and remote work
sections.tags: remote, hybrid, work from home, wfh, office days, home office, stipend, core hours, time zone, internet, coworking, work location, schedule, flexible, out of state
sections.body:
Meridian Works is hybrid. Most teams are in the office two or three days a week, usually Tuesday to Thursday, and some roles are fully remote. Your offer letter states which applies to you.

Core hours: 10:00am to 3:00pm in your local time zone. Be reachable for meetings during those hours. Outside them, your schedule is flexible as long as your work gets done and your team can rely on you.
Anchor days: teams choose which days to be in the office together. Tuesday to Thursday is the default. Ask your manager what your team does.

Working from a different location: you can work remotely from your home city or from any state where we are registered as an employer. Working from a different state for more than 2 weeks needs manager and People approval because of tax and payroll rules. Ask People before you plan long stays away from your work location.

Home-office setup: a one-time $500 stipend for equipment such as a monitor, chair or desk. Claim it through Ramp within 90 days of your start date.
Internet: fully remote employees can expense up to $50 per month for home internet.
Coworking: fully remote employees who live within 20 miles of a coworking space may expense up to $100 per month for it, with manager approval.
Equipment ownership: anything the company pays for stays company property. Return it when you leave, except items under $100.

Working remotely well: keep your calendar accurate, turn on video for team meetings when you can, write things down so people in other time zones can catch up, and take your time off.
Security while remote: use the company VPN on public Wi-Fi, keep your screen private, and never work on customer data in a public place where others can see the screen.
Ergonomics: ask People about a free ergonomic assessment if you have pain or discomfort. It is a health and safety matter, not a perk.

sections.title: Communication norms
sections.tags: slack, email, response time, channels, dm, urgent, etiquette, communication, all-hands, time zones, status, notifications, messaging
sections.body:
Slack: use channels instead of DMs for anything others might need to see later. Naming: #team-, #proj-, #help-, #cust- (customer channels; only for approved staff) and #social-. Keep threads in threads.
Response times: expect a reply within one business day. If it is urgent, say "urgent" in the first line and tag the person. For real emergencies (outage, security incident, safety), page through PagerDuty or call, do not rely on Slack.
Email: used mainly for customers, vendors and formal announcements.
Be findable: set your Slack status when you are out, in focus time, or in a different time zone. Use Do Not Disturb outside your working hours. Nobody is expected to reply at night or on weekends.
Write it down: for decisions that affect more than one team, write a short doc in Notion (context, options and a recommendation), then ask for comments for 3 business days.
Time zones: post meeting times in Eastern and your local time. Try not to schedule anything before 8:00am or after 5:00pm for the person you are inviting.
Company all-hands: the first Thursday of every month at 11:00am Central, recorded for anyone who cannot attend. Leaders share company results and take anonymous questions.
Friday Notes: a short weekly post in #general from each department with wins, launches and what is coming.
Tone: assume good intent, be specific, and thank people. Avoid sarcasm in writing. It does not travel well.
Confidential topics: never discuss pay disputes, performance concerns or personal matters in public channels.

sections.title: Meetings and calendars
sections.tags: meetings, agenda, 25 minutes, 50 minutes, calendar, decline meeting, no meeting, focus time, 1:1, standup, meeting rules, recurring
sections.body:
Length: default to 25 or 50 minutes so people have time to breathe between calls.
Agenda: every meeting has an agenda in the invite. You can decline a meeting without one, politely, and ask for the agenda.
Owner: every meeting has one named owner who starts on time, keeps notes and records decisions and actions.
Notes: post notes in the relevant channel or Notion page within 24 hours. If a meeting produced no decision or action, it probably should have been a message.
No-meeting time: Wednesday afternoons are meeting-free company-wide for focus time (except customer meetings and incidents).
1:1s: weekly, 30 minutes, with your manager. It is your meeting, so bring the agenda. Do not cancel it without rescheduling.
Standups: teams choose their own format. Many squads use a short async standup in Slack instead of a live one.
Recurring meetings: review them each quarter. If nobody needs one, delete it.
Video: cameras on is encouraged for small meetings but never required. Join by phone if you need to.
Interviews and customer calls: do not double-book these. If something clashes, ask for a reschedule as early as you can.
Calendar hygiene: keep working locations and out-of-office entries current, and mark private appointments as private.

sections.title: Decision-making and planning
sections.tags: okr, okrs, planning, goals, quarterly planning, daci, dri, decision, roadmap, priorities, rfc, proposal, quarter
sections.body:
OKRs: we set company, team and individual objectives and key results every quarter. Company OKRs are shared at the start-of-quarter all-hands. Team OKRs are in Notion. You should be able to point to your OKRs and say how your work connects to a company OKR.
Planning calendar: planning weeks are the last two weeks of each quarter. Roadmaps are reviewed monthly. Do not plan on taking time off during planning weeks unless it is unavoidable, and tell your manager early.
Scoring: at quarter end teams score OKRs from 0.0 to 1.0. A 0.7 is a good result. If you score 1.0 every time, your goals were probably not ambitious enough.

DRI: every task and decision has one directly responsible individual. If it is unclear who that is, the first job is to settle that.
DACI: for decisions that involve more than one team, use DACI: the Driver runs the process, the Approver decides, Contributors give input, and Informed people are told. Write it in a Notion decision doc.
Engineering RFCs: significant technical changes start with an RFC posted for comment for at least 5 business days.
Disagree and commit: once a decision is made, everyone supports it, even if they argued for something else. Raise concerns before the decision, and again if you learn something new afterward.
Reversible vs irreversible: move fast on decisions you can undo, and slow down on ones you cannot.

sections.title: Performance reviews and feedback
sections.tags: performance review, review cycle, june, december, self review, peer feedback, calibration, rating, feedback, pip, performance improvement, review dates, manager review
sections.body:
Cadence: formal reviews twice a year, in June and December. They combine a self-review, peer feedback and a manager review, and are used to talk about growth, not just ratings.

December 2026 cycle (dates):
- Monday, November 30: self-review opens.
- Monday, December 7: self-reviews due.
- Wednesday, December 9: peer feedback due.
- Monday, December 14: manager reviews due.
- December 14 to 18: calibration (managers compare results across teams for fairness).
- January 5 to 16, 2027: review conversations with your manager.
Because of the holiday closure from December 24 to 28, do not leave your self-review until the last day.

Ratings: a 5-point scale from "Needs improvement" to "Outstanding". The middle rating, "Solid contributor", is the most common and is a good rating.
Peer feedback: you nominate 3 to 5 colleagues and your manager may add some. Feedback is written to be constructive and specific. Your manager summarizes themes. It is not shared word for word.
Feedback all year: give and ask for feedback often. Use the "situation, behavior, impact" pattern: what happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
Struggling: if you are struggling, tell your manager early. Struggling early is normal.
Performance concerns: if your performance is below expectations, your manager will tell you in writing, explain what "good" looks like, and give a clear plan with support and a timeline, typically 30 to 60 days (a performance improvement plan, or PIP). A PIP is a serious step, but it is meant to help you succeed. You can ask People to sit in on any of these meetings.
Disagreeing with your review: talk with your manager first. If that doesn't resolve it, contact People within 2 weeks of receiving your review.

sections.title: Career growth and levels
sections.tags: promotion, levels, career ladder, growth, e1, e2, e3, e4, e5, e6, senior, staff, manager track, ic track, promotion cycle, career development, internal transfer
sections.body:
Career ladders: each function has a written ladder in Notion describing expectations at each level. Ask your manager for the ladder for your role.
Engineering example: E1 (entry), E2 (engineer), E3 (senior), E4 (staff), E5 (principal), E6 (distinguished). Similar ladders exist for Product, Design, Sales, Customer Success, Marketing and Operations.
Two tracks: individual contributor (IC) and manager. Moving between them is allowed. Managers are not "higher" than ICs at equal levels.

Promotions: decided twice a year, in the March and September cycles. Promotion is based on sustained performance at the next level (usually 6 months or more), not potential. Your manager nominates you with a written case, and a committee reviews it. You do not have to be nominated by a certain time, but talk to your manager at least 3 months before a cycle if you want to be considered.
Current cycle: the September 2026 promotion cycle is underway. Nominations have closed and decisions are shared with managers in October.

Growth conversations: talk with your manager about growth in every quarter, not just at review time.
Internal moves: after 12 months in a role you can apply for internal openings without your manager's permission. Tell them as a courtesy. Openings are posted in #open-roles and the internal jobs page.
Learning: use your $1,000 learning budget (see Benefits: wellbeing, learning and perks), the monthly lunch-and-learns in #learning, and the leadership program for new managers.
New managers: everyone who becomes a manager completes the 8-week Managing at Meridian program.

sections.title: Manager handbook: the essentials
sections.tags: manager, managers, managing, 1:1, people manager, direct reports, approvals, team lead, how to manage, new manager, responsibilities, supervisor
sections.body:
This section is for people managers. Employees should read it too, so they know what to expect from their manager.

Your core responsibilities:
- Weekly 30-minute 1:1s with each direct report. Let them set the agenda. Write down commitments and follow up.
- Clear goals. Agree OKRs each quarter, and make sure each person can explain how their work supports a company priority.
- Regular feedback. Give specific feedback within a few days, rather than saving it for the review. Praise in public, correct in private.
- Growth. Talk about career growth every quarter, not just at review time.
- Fairness. Apply the same standards to everyone. Watch for bias in who gets stretch projects and praise.

Approvals that you handle: time off (within 2 business days), expenses from $100 to $1,000, overtime for non-exempt team members, learning budget requests, access requests for customer data, and software requests. Do not approve your own requests. Your manager does.

Things you must involve People in: any leave request beyond normal PTO, accommodation requests, performance plans (PIPs), disciplinary steps, resignations and terminations, complaints about behavior, and changes to pay or level. Always call People before you act on a concern, not after.
What you must pass to People: any report of harassment, discrimination or retaliation, within 2 business days. You cannot keep it confidential.
Do not: discuss one person's pay, performance or health with others, ask about health conditions, promise raises or promotions, or make decisions about leave without People.
Support for you: new managers complete the 8-week Managing at Meridian program within their first 90 days. People partners are available for any "how do I handle this?" conversation.

sections.title: Manager handbook: hiring and interviewing
sections.tags: hiring, interviewing, recruiting, candidates, scorecard, job posting, offer, interview panel, recruiter, headcount approval, structured interview, hiring process
sections.body:
Headcount: every new role needs approved headcount in the annual plan or approval from the VP and the CFO. No job is posted until it is approved. Backfills need VP approval.
Steps for every hire:
1. Write a role scorecard with the outcomes, skills and values you are looking for. People's recruiters help.
2. Post the role with a salary range (required in several states and in our policy everywhere).
3. Screen: a recruiter call, then a hiring manager call.
4. Interview loop: 3 to 5 interviews, each assigned a specific skill from the scorecard. Every panelist completes interviewer training first.
5. Written feedback: panelists submit scores and notes in the applicant tracking system before they see anyone else's feedback. This avoids anchoring.
6. Debrief: the panel meets, reviews evidence against the scorecard and decides. The hiring manager makes the final decision with the recruiter.
7. References and background check: with the candidate's consent, after a verbal offer.
8. Offer: People prepares it within the salary band. Offers above the band need VP and People approval. Give candidates at least 5 business days to decide.

Rules of fair hiring: ask every candidate the same core questions. Never ask about age, marital or family status, pregnancy, religion, disability, health, nationality or citizenship. Do not ask about current or past pay (in many places this is illegal). Stick to the scorecard.
Candidate experience: respond to every candidate within 2 business days of each stage, and give timely, respectful feedback. A rejected candidate may be a future customer or colleague.
Referrals: flag referrals in the system. Referred candidates get the same process. The referrer should not sit on the panel.
Timeline: target 25 days from application to offer. The recruiter tracks this.

sections.title: Recognition, community and employee groups
sections.tags: erg, employee resource group, recognition, kudos, spot bonus, social events, community, holiday party, retreat, diversity, inclusion, belonging, referral, referral bonus, volunteer

Recognition: give shout-outs in #kudos. Anyone can nominate a colleague each quarter for a Meridian Moments award tied to one of our values. Managers can also award a spot bonus of up to $250 with People approval for exceptional work.

Employee resource groups (ERGs): open to everyone, including allies.
